top_story: The Houthi advance across Yemen’s Red Sea coast by 11 September had already shifted the regional balance toward Iran-aligned forces, and their capture of a strategic island near Bab al-Mandab on 12 September turned that momentum into direct leverage over one of the world’s most sensitive oil and shipping chokepoints. That battlefield gain quickly widened the crisis beyond Yemen, leaving Washington and Gulf states with fewer good options as a local front acquired clear regional coercive value. By early 13 September, attacks on ships in Hormuz and inside Saudi Arabia showed the pressure campaign extending across both the Red Sea and Gulf corridors, sharpening risks to energy flows and raising costs for civilians whose livelihoods depend on trade stability. The core development is not only Houthi territorial expansion, but the emergence of an Iran-linked ability to menace multiple maritime arteries at once, deepening regional insecurity and economic vulnerability.
